hints: Focus on what atomisation really means, turning an element into separate gaseous atoms.
Remember bromine is a liquid in its standard state at 298 K, so you must start from $\text{Br}_2(l)$.
Check how many moles of gaseous atoms are made, the definition requires exactly one mole of $\text{Br}(g)$.
walkthrough:
**Recall the definition of atomisation**

Think of atomisation as pulling an element completely apart into single, free atoms in the gas phase.

Definition:
$$\text{element in standard state} \rightarrow 1 \text{ mol of gaseous atoms}$$

**Find the standard state of bromine**

Bromine is one of the few elements that is liquid at standard conditions of 298 K and 1 atm.

So we must start from $\text{Br}_2(l)$, not $\text{Br}_2(g)$.

**Fix the moles to make one atom**

We need exactly $1$ mol of $\text{Br}(g)$ as product.

Since each $\text{Br}_2$ gives two Br atoms, we need only half a mole of it:
$$\frac{1}{2}\text{Br}_2(l) \rightarrow \text{Br}(g)$$

options.A: Starts correctly from $\text{Br}_2(l)$ but makes $2$ mol of $\text{Br}(g)$. Atomisation enthalpy is defined per $1$ mol of gaseous atoms, so this is double the correct amount.
options.B: Makes $2$ mol of atoms and also starts from the wrong state, $\text{Br}_2(g)$. This is actually the bond dissociation of gaseous bromine, not atomisation from the standard state.
options.C: Perfect match. It starts from the standard state $\text{Br}_2(l)$ and produces exactly $1$ mol of $\text{Br}(g)$. This is the definition of standard enthalpy of atomisation of bromine.
options.D: Has the correct $1$ mol of product but starts from $\text{Br}_2(g)$. The standard state of bromine is liquid, so you must include the change from liquid to atoms.
